title: Open the millihertz gravitational-wave sky as a working observatory

concept.text: The innovation is a space observatory that routinely detects and characterizes gravitational waves in the millihertz frequency range, turning that part of the sky into a sustained source of astronomical measurements. The intended advance extends beyond an isolated detection: it requires calibrated observations, characterization of individual sources and repeated observations sufficient to study source populations. Millihertz coverage is part of the concept being proposed; the supplied ESA summaries do not independently establish its frequency specification.

ESA’s LISA material documents the underlying goal of a space-based gravitational-wave observatory and identifies a spacecraft architecture using laser beams. The proposed measurement principle involves exceptionally quiet free-falling test masses and precise tracking of changing separations between spacecraft. Those technical requirements remain part of the supplied research’s explanation, rather than requirements substantiated by the retained ESA summaries.

A working scientific observatory must be distinguished from a mission that tests enabling technology. ESA describes LISA Pathfinder as a technology demonstration for gravitational-wave detection and LISA as the planned observatory. Successful technology testing would be an enabling step, while completion of this innovation would require sustained astronomical observations.

significance.text: Conditional scientific significance: if routine millihertz observations provide access to a gravitational-wave band beyond the reach of current ground-based observatories, they would add a major astronomical observing capability. Repeated measurements could turn individual events into comparative studies of sources and populations. The supplied summaries do not establish the claimed frequency-band comparison, so that premise remains qualified rather than demonstrated here.

ESA identifies collisions and mergers of supermassive black holes as a scientific target of the planned observatory. Observing and characterizing such systems would provide a direct scientific use for the capability. This is a documented mission objective, not a report of achieved detections or a guarantee of what the observatory will discover.

Conditional downstream possibilities include studying long-lived compact binaries, investigating massive black-hole populations and using suitable signals to test gravitational physics. Long-lived compact-binary population studies are proposed in the research but are not established by the supplied source summaries. More broadly, opening an observing band would provide measurements with which to investigate these questions; it would not by itself settle black-hole formation histories, establish a failure of general relativity or identify a primordial gravitational-wave background. Detectable sources and the conclusions they support remain empirical questions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an integrated space instrument that converts precision measurement technology into reliable millihertz gravitational-wave astronomy. The research identifies quiet free-falling test masses and measurements of tiny changes in spacecraft separation as central requirements. In engineering terms, the proposed system must keep unwanted test-mass motion and measurement disturbances sufficiently controlled and understood that astronomical signals can be distinguished from instrument behavior. The supplied summaries do not quantify the required quietness, displacement sensitivity or frequency-dependent noise.

The research attributes the difficulty of making these measurements on Earth to ground motion and fluctuating gravity. These remain proposed explanations requiring further technical evidence in this record: the retained ESA material does not describe either noise mechanism or establish the terrestrial sensitivity limit. Their absence from these summaries does not show that the explanation is false, but it prevents a supported quantitative account of why the specified space configuration is necessary.

Proposed engineering and analysis barriers also include validating calibration, establishing a credible noise model, demonstrating stable performance over an extended observing period and extracting reproducible source properties. These are the practical steps connecting an instrument that measures changing separations to an observatory that supports population science. ESA’s distinction between Pathfinder’s technology role and LISA’s observatory role supports that separation of milestones, although the supplied summaries do not specify acceptance thresholds for them.

current_state.text: ESA describes LISA Pathfinder as a technology-demonstration mission intended to establish that technology needed for LISA would function in space. The retained overview establishes this mission role but does not report measured free-fall precision. Consequently, the earlier research statement that Pathfinder demonstrated the relevant precision free-fall performance cannot be verified from the supplied material. This evidentiary limitation does not establish that the performance result was false or that the mission failed.

The retained ESA LISA page lists launch as planned for 2035 and describes the observatory as forthcoming. A construction-announcement summary dated 17 June 2025 identifies supermassive black-hole mergers as a target. Neither the launch plan nor the announcement establishes an operating millihertz observatory, achieved gravitational-wave detections or completed population science.

The timing and coverage of this evidence constrain the assessment. Both ESA pages are undated mission overviews retrieved on 11 November 2026, after the review’s 1 November 2026 assessment date, and the supplied review reports an empty bounded-search record for freshness verification. The retained page therefore supports reporting the 2035 schedule as listed, but cannot independently establish the exact mission status or schedule on the earlier assessment date.

The source index records saved HTML artifacts without reported extraction errors or truncation, while the evidence review characterizes the retained evidence as partial and the Pathfinder overview as repetitive. These describe different limitations: a successfully saved page can still omit the technical results needed to evaluate a claim. The supplied material does not provide measured sensitivity curves, achieved free-fall precision or observational results sufficient to establish completion.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a space instrument in a declared millihertz observing range and validate its calibration and noise model against observations. A convincing assessment would specify the frequency coverage, sensitivity, calibration uncertainty and observing duration over which the instrument supports its scientific claims. These are proposed acceptance dimensions, not established standards or requirements attributed to ESA; numerical thresholds remain to be defined.
completion_criteria.label: Millihertz space observations validate instrument calibration and noise model

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: detect and characterize multiple individually resolved gravitational-wave sources, with documented uncertainty estimates and checks that the signals are distinguishable from instrumental disturbances. Reproducibility should include independent analysis of the available observations and calibration information, producing consistent detections and source properties within stated uncertainties. The required number and diversity of sources should be justified against the intended science rather than assigned an arbitrary universal threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Multiple resolved gravitational-wave sources yield independently reproducible characterizations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: sustain observations long enough to establish repeatable population science, with explicit treatment of sensitivity, source-selection effects and the limits of the observing period. Completion should establish the range of frequencies, source types and operating conditions actually demonstrated. A finite observing campaign can establish useful breadth and reliability; it cannot prove access to every millihertz source or guarantee answers to every associated scientific question.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained observations establish repeatable population science with explicit limits

related_concepts.text: Conceptual relationship to AST-05, “Detect and identify a primordial gravitational-wave background”: both concern gravitational-wave astronomy, but their endpoints differ. AST-10 establishes an observing capability; AST-05 requires detecting a background and establishing its primordial origin. A working observatory could provide relevant measurements if its demonstrated coverage and sensitivity permit, but neither resolved-source detections nor observatory operation would establish a primordial background.

Conceptual relationship to AST-07, “Discover a reproducible breakdown of general relativity near black holes”: sufficiently informative black-hole observations could support tests of gravitational theory. AST-10 would provide an instrument and observations; AST-07 requires a reproducible physical discrepancy with an adequately established interpretation. Routine gravitational-wave astronomy could succeed even if all measured signals remain consistent with general relativity.

Conceptual relationship to AST-13, “Establish how the earliest massive black holes formed and grew”: ESA’s documented black-hole merger target provides a potential observational connection. Whether those observations can resolve the origins and growth of the earliest massive black holes depends on the sources detected and the conclusions their measurements support. AST-13 remains a distinct explanatory achievement rather than an automatic consequence of completing AST-10.

Conceptual relationship to AST-09, “Make neutrino astronomy capable of routinely resolving hidden cosmic sources”: both seek to turn difficult measurements into repeatable astronomical observations. They concern different messengers, instruments and source-identification problems. AST-12, “Directly detect the cosmic neutrino background,” has a different endpoint again: detecting a particular background rather than establishing routine resolved-source astronomy. These entries remain separate capabilities and discoveries.

unresolved_issues: The supplied summaries do not independently establish millihertz frequency coverage, quantitative sensitivity requirements or the comparison with ground-based observatories.
Measured Pathfinder free-fall performance and its relationship to the proposed observatory requirements remain unverified within this record.
The terrestrial ground-motion and fluctuating-gravity explanation requires technical evidence beyond the retained summaries.
Long-lived compact-binary population studies remain a proposed scientific use without specific support in the supplied source summaries.
The exact mission status and launch schedule on 1 November 2026 cannot be independently reconstructed from the later-retrieved, undated pages.

Quantitative acceptance thresholds for calibration, noise validation, source characterization, observing duration and population science remain to be justified. The review’s recommendation for measurable thresholds is adopted as a requirement to define them, without inventing values.

brief.title: Watching the universe through ripples in space
possible: Astronomers could routinely study gravitational waves—ripples in space and time—from space. The observatory would measure waves in the millihertz range, where the ripples repeat slowly, and turn repeated detections into reliable measurements of individual sources.
why: Astronomers could study supermassive black holes colliding and merging. Repeated observations would let them compare sources and study whole populations, extending what they can learn from individual events.

sources.showed: ESA operated LISA Pathfinder in space as a technology demonstration for gravitational-wave detection.
sources.cited_for: LISA Pathfinder represents the technology-testing step toward a space observatory.
sources.not_established: Operating a technology demonstrator does not establish routine astronomical detections or measurements of source populations.

sources.showed: ESA approved LISA and signed an agreement to build it. The planned observatory uses spacecraft linked by laser beams and targets merging supermassive black holes.
sources.cited_for: LISA provides a planned route to observing gravitational waves from space.
sources.not_established: Mission approval and a construction agreement do not demonstrate the required sensitivity or sustained astronomical observations.

shown: ESA has operated LISA Pathfinder to test technology for detecting gravitational waves. Its planned LISA observatory has reached a construction agreement, with launch planned for 2035. Sustained astronomical measurements remain the next scientific achievement.
missing: An operating space instrument must distinguish the intended slow gravitational waves from unwanted motion and measurement disturbances.
Reliable source measurements must survive independent analysis with their uncertainties accounted for.
Sustained observations must support repeatable studies of source populations while accounting for sources the instrument misses.

milestones.label: Space measurements establish instrument accuracy and unwanted disturbances
milestones.explanation: Observations in the intended millihertz range would have to establish measurement accuracy and explain unwanted disturbances. This would make astronomical signals distinguishable from instrument behavior.

milestones.label: Independent analyses agree on multiple individual sources
milestones.explanation: Independent analyses would have to recover multiple distinct sources and agree on their properties within stated uncertainties. This would establish reliable astronomical measurements.

milestones.label: Sustained observations yield repeatable population studies
milestones.explanation: Extended observations would have to yield repeatable population studies that account for missed sources and observing limits. This would establish a working observatory with a clear scientific reach.

uncertain: The required sensitivity, measurement accuracy and observing duration still need justified thresholds.
The number and variety of sources needed to establish success depend on the intended science.
Which sources will be detectable, and what they will reveal about black holes and gravity, remain open questions.

page.title: Millihertz gravitational-wave observatory
page.definition: A space observatory detects gravitational waves—oscillations of spacetime—in the millihertz frequency band using laser interferometry between freely falling reference bodies. Repeated observations resolve individual sources and measure source populations.

goal.need: LISA’s specified measurement band is 0.1 mHz–1 Hz. It covers compact stellar binaries with orbital periods of minutes to hours and mergers of massive black holes. Measurements in this band address binary evolution, black-hole growth and gravity in a frequency regime between those probed by pulsar timing and ground-based interferometers.

completion.title: A space observatory measures about 5000 Galactic binary periods to better than one part per million.
completion.criterion: Distinguish about 5000 Galactic compact binaries using gravitational-wave observations from space and infer each orbital period P with relative precision δP/P < 10⁻⁶, fulfilling observational requirement OR 1.1.a.

completion.basis: ESA links this requirement to surveying the period distribution of Galactic binaries. It supplies a population-measurement benchmark. This is one specified LISA science requirement; satisfying it does not establish achievement of every mission objective.

milestones.title: A laboratory interferometer measures test-mass displacement with noise below 9 pm/√Hz at 3–30 mHz.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate displacement-readout noise below 9 pm/√Hz between 3 and 30 mHz with simulated test-mass angular motion. A laboratory experiment using two articulated mirrors on the LISA Technology Package engineering optical bench demonstrated the required resolution after subtracting angular coupling; the paper was published on 5 February 2008.
milestones.set_by: ESA LISA Technology Package programme; interferometer requirements reported by its metrology developers in Guzmán Cervantes et al.

milestones.title: Two test masses in space have relative acceleration noise below 30 fm s⁻²/√Hz at 1 mHz.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate differential acceleration noise below the Pathfinder design target of 30 fm s⁻²/√Hz at 1 mHz. Pathfinder’s two 1.928 kg test masses achieved 5.2 ± 0.1 fm s⁻²/√Hz over 0.7–20 mHz, reported on 7 June 2016. A follow-up published on 5 February 2018 extended noise measurements down to 20 μHz. Pathfinder operated from 1 March 2016 to 30 June 2017.
